children: After months of military and trade conflicts, investors might expect an impact on the stock market. It hasn't happened.

Stocks have pushed past a rocky start to the third quarter and are continuing their upward trajectory. The S&P 500 isn't far from its record close reached in mid-August, putting it up nearly 13% this year. The Nasdaq Composite has risen about 14% since the start of the year.

Yet perhaps the market is right to overlook the ongoing tensions, notes Doug Peta, head of essentials at BCA Research. Wall Street's complacency appears to be all about the health of the economy, earnings, and the artificial-intelligence trade-and not relentless geopolitical uncertainty.

"The Trump administration's impatience with military, trade and bond market developments is more of a reflection of Republicans' fraught midterm prospects than a commentary on the U.S. economy, which is doing fine," he said.

Employment remains relatively strong, with the unemployment rate running at 4.1%-even though many consumers are feeling less downbeat about jobs. In addition, corporate earnings are still growing at a double-digit clip in percent terms.

While the Iran war might be more intractable than bulls had hoped, it could be reaching a point where both sides feel inclined to lower the temperature. Plus, Wall Street will likely remain unfazed if earnings and the artificial-intelligence trade are robust.

"With the Trump administration in need of a diplomatic breakthrough to ease near-term inflation pressures and Iranian leaders potentially wearying of withstanding U.S. pressure, the two sides may be ready to throttle down hostilities, giving global rates markets a break," he notes.

Iran obviously could keep oil prices high by throttling crude's transit, but Peta notes that private U.S. inventories of oil have been on the rise. That means more than the official ship tracking totals could be leaving the Gulf region, which could be good news for a market still concerned about inflation.

Elsewhere, Peta doesn't think any wind down in the war will be an issue for global defense spending, which could bolster stocks in that sector. Although ceasefires in the wars in Ukraine and Iran may materialize in the next year or two, that will only be a temporary setback for the sector.

With the U.S. stepping back from its position as postwar peacekeeper, a new more multipolar world paradigm is likely to emerge, with individual nations jockeying to ramp up their own defense capabilities. Peta says the European Union and Japan are both already ramping up their defense spending as tensions rise in their backyards.
The increasing use of drones make that an area where investment is likely to keep chugging ahead, much as Barron's reported earlier this summer.

Another positive for the stock market: The clock doesn't seem to be running down for the AI trade, which has bolstered so much of the recent stock market rally. Earlier this week, sector bellwether Nvidia's report highlighted ongoing strong demand in the space.
In addition, recent economic growth confirms that the stock market's gains are more than just an AI story.

"We remain constructive on risk assets in the near term and are willing to remain fully invested into a blow-off rally crescendo but are vigilant for signs that the bull market has gone too far," Peta says.
That seems to be a problem for another day.
